# Ten-plant model comparison — 12 September 2026

**The experiment is complete: ten plants × six settings = 60 original outputs.** They were generated by OpenAI subscription subagents, as requested, with no separately billed model API calls. Each received the same frozen prompt and source packets, with no access to the editorial examples or another model's outputs.

Open the [side-by-side review page](../data/analysis/plant-content-v1/benchmark/review.html) to select a plant and compare any two models. It includes the paragraphs, all extracted facts, food/toxicity details, review flags, original JSON and source passages. Original results are in [the results directory](../data/analysis/plant-content-v1/benchmark/results/).

My reading is that **Astra at maximum reasoning handled source qualifications best in this pilot**, while **Sol at high reasoning is the most promising next candidate to test for a cheaper production pass**. The lower-cost models can produce readable paragraphs, but mistakes inside the structured facts would make them hard to trust without substantial checking. This is a small development comparison, not a measured population error rate or proof that any model is ready for unattended publication.

## Output size and observed differences

Every setting produced eight paragraphs, withheld the broader-taxon Ranunculus case for review, and returned insufficient source for the empty Cistus packet. All 60 outputs passed the automated shape and passage-ID checks. Manual inspection nevertheless found unsupported claims and references to passages that exist but do not support the attached fact.

Means below cover the **same eight nonempty drafts**, excluding the two expected abstentions. Counts use compact JSON and `o200k_base`; they are visible-text measurements, not agent billing usage.

| Model / reasoning | Mean paragraph tokens | Mean complete record tokens | Findings from this run |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| GPT-5.6 Luna / low | 75 | 366 | Some unsupported details and poor evidence linking; misses useful context |
| GPT-5.6 Luna / high | 83 | 633 | Extracts more, but introduces a direction error when summarising a correct fact |
| GPT-5.6 Terra / low | 78 | 441 | Generally readable; a material food-part extraction error |
| GPT-5.6 Terra / high | 83 | 459 | Avoids that food-part error, but still drops qualifications and distinctive material |
| GPT-5.6 Sol / high | 78 | 520 | Better selection and warning handling; remaining scope and source-only issues |
| GPT-6 Astra / max | 80 | 619 | Most careful with historical scope, uncertain attribution and explicit warnings |

More reasoning did not consistently increase quality, and more output did not imply more accuracy. Luna high produced a larger average record than Astra max. The prose itself stayed small across all six settings; extracted facts and qualifications dominate visible output size.

## Concrete findings to inspect

**Cook pine — selecting and explaining an interesting fact.** The source's `s1:p6` describes a 2017 study: southward lean in the Northern Hemisphere and northward lean in the Southern Hemisphere. Luna low and both Terra runs omitted the leaning finding entirely. Luna high stored the directions correctly in fact `f5`, then described the direction confusingly as towards a pole in the paragraph. Sol and Astra retained the finding and described it correctly. This is a good test of both editorial selection and consistency between facts and prose.

**Oxalis — food parts and source warnings.** Terra low's food-use entry lists bulbs and petals as food. In `s1:p20`, bulbs are mentioned for folk treatment of worms and petals for yellow dye; neither passage establishes those parts as food. Luna high labels the stew ingredient “whole plant” even though `s1:p19` leaves the part unspecified. Sol and Astra preserve the distinction more carefully, although Sol also uses a nonspecific “plant” label. Astra explicitly calls the stew parts unspecified, separates dye use, preserves the original-research warning and distinguishes disputed human claims from the livestock reports. Neither model validates those hazard claims merely by extracting them.

**Sour fig — a valid evidence ID can still be wrong.** Luna low's identity and origin facts point to `s1:p1`, which contains only a date-formatting template. The relevant description is in `s1:p2` and `s1:p4`. Its “perennial” label is also not explicitly established in those selected passages. The automatic checker correctly confirms only that `s1:p1` exists; it cannot establish factual support. Terra high and Luna high both omit the explicit citation-needed warning attached to the fruit/jam sentence. Sol and Astra preserve it.

**Cork oak — animals are not people.** All six correctly avoided turning pig feeding into human edibility. Luna low's paragraph calls the harvested material “living bark”, an imprecise description given the source's explicit explanation in `s1:p36` that cork consists of dead cells. The stronger summaries explain regeneration without that wording. Some records still overstate fire survival rather than consistently saying the bark helps the tree survive.

**Bee orchid — distribution, reproduction and food attribution.** Luna low, Luna high and Terra low label an occurrence description from `s1:p6` as `native_range`, although that passage does not explicitly distinguish native from introduced occurrence. Sol, Astra and Terra high avoid that field. Sol and both Terra runs correctly retain regional self-pollination differences; the Luna summaries leave out northern self-pollination. Astra also distinguishes the species-attributed historical salep claim from the paragraph's generic modern salep discussion and flags the need for attribution review. Sol and both Terra runs carry the historical claim into modern species food use without that distinction. Sol adds the common designation “long-horned” for the bee, which the supplied passage does not itself provide; under this strict source-only experiment that wording should be removed or supported.

**Armeria — a historical national assessment.** Every model retained a date and national conservation scope somewhere. Some lower-tier prose nevertheless starts with a present-tense single-locality claim before giving the old assessment. Sol and Astra anchor the historical count more clearly. Astra explicitly distinguishes the historical regional assessment from current/global status. The one-adult count is a statement in the saved assessment, not something we have verified about today's population.

**Strawberry tree — whether to extract a dubious anecdote.** Astra retained the Irish-origin uncertainty directly in the native-range fact. It also noticed the citation-needed anecdote about bears becoming intoxicated by fermented fruit and recorded it under toxicity, with the organism and warning. That is faithful capture of a source claim, but it exposes a presentation risk: a future generic “toxic” badge must not be derived from `toxicity.status` alone. Evidence strength, affected organism and fermentation conditions matter. The strongest model's extra extraction is not automatically useful reader-facing content.

**Sparse and mismatched sources.** All models avoided inventing food or toxicity claims for the short nightshade packet and withheld unsupported paragraphs for the two gap/scope cases. These are useful successes, but relatively easy cases. Testing harder name/scope ambiguities will be necessary before trusting a routing rule.

## What to change before another round

Keep v1 and these outputs frozen as a baseline. The next prompt/schema version should:

1. Require each cited passage to support the particular attached claim, and require every summary claim to be represented in the extracted record. Existing IDs alone are not sufficient.
2. Make native origin distinct from occurrence, and preserve the date in both the fact and the sentence whenever a population count or assessment is historical.
3. Store separate food-use entries for each part/use/condition; use null for an unspecified plant part. Medicinal use, dye use and animal feed must not populate human food parts.
4. Carry claim-level warning flags as structured metadata, alongside the original wording and evidence. Keep uncertainty attached when a field is reused elsewhere.
5. Distinguish `not_documented` after reading a relevant source from `not_assessed` for unreviewed or absent evidence. Several runs treated them interchangeably.
6. Add a suitable reproductive-trait category rather than forcing every reproductive detail into flowering or life cycle; Terra high, for example, filed conifer cone morphology under flowering.
7. Encourage accessible explanation of a distinctive supported trait over routine measurements or garden-use boilerplate. Avoid specialist terms such as “labellum”, “pollinia” and “hydromorphism” unless explained.

The comparison supports keeping **Sol high as a candidate baseline and Astra max as a reference for difficult cases**, while testing a revised prompt against the inexpensive models again. It does not yet demonstrate that automatic escalation can reliably identify every error. A fresh held-out sample should follow our review of these paragraphs. We have not run a second round or generated the full catalogue.

## Costs and limits of this experiment

There were no external paid model API requests. Subscription subagents do not expose the API input, cached-input or hidden-reasoning token counters needed to calculate actual API cost. Each agent processed ten plants in one task with system and tool context; this differs from ten independent production requests. Only one run per setting was made. The comparison does not isolate model capacity from all effects of sampling and agent execution.

Current published standard API text prices give the scale of the eventual choice:

| Model | Input / million tokens | Output / million tokens |
|---|---:|---:|
| [GPT-5.6 Luna](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-5.6-luna) | $0.20 | $1.20 |
| [GPT-5.6 Terra](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-5.6-terra) | $2.00 | $12.00 |
| [GPT-5.6 Sol](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-5.6-sol) | $4.00 | $20.00 |
| [GPT-6 Astra](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-6-astra) | $10.00 | $50.00 |

Checked 12 September 2026. These are published API rates, **not charges incurred by this experiment**. Sol's page describes its rate as promotional through at least 21 November 2026. Cached reads/writes and any batch rates require separate accounting. [Hidden reasoning tokens are billed as output](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/reasoning); the visible 520- or 619-token record is therefore not the complete output cost of a reasoning-model API request.

For planning, the [full-corpus census](plant-content-pilot.md) gives 10.04M draft input tokens for the 6,142 name-matched species before API overhead. The current ten-plant comparison deliberately includes rich articles and failure cases, so multiplying its average output by every species would be a scenario, not a measured population estimate. We now have a solid input baseline and real output examples; the remaining cost uncertainty is model-specific tokenisation, reasoning usage, retries and the final field/template choices.

## Files and checks

The [frozen configuration](../config/plant-content-benchmark-v1.json) lists all ten taxa, model/settings and the prompt hash. The [prompt](../config/plant-content-prompt-v1.txt), source packet copies, raw model JSON and [validation/count report](../data/analysis/plant-content-v1/benchmark/validation.json) remain available for inspection. The parent reviewed every output against its supplied passages; this is editorial source checking, not independent botanical fact verification.

Validation: all 60 records present, all passage pointers resolve structurally, 11 cleaner/validation tests pass, census totals and frozen hashes agree, and the local review page was tested across all 60 selectable outputs with navigation and a mobile viewport. The existing 176 stories and 300-taxon review set also pass their original offline consistency check.

Rebuild the viewer with `.venv/bin/python scripts/render_plant_model_comparison.py`. Recount/check original results with `.venv/bin/python scripts/review_plant_content_pilot.py --benchmark`. Neither command calls a model or edits its output.
